On this form, you can create, view, and edit barcode standards. Barcode standards are an intermediary to allow you to set identifiers to your industry standards barcodes. An example of a standard is GS1 barcodes. Further, GS1 Application Identifiers (AIs) are prefixes used in barcodes and EPC/RFID-tags to define the meaning and format of data attributes. This tool was developed in response to the growing use of AIs in the various industry sectors to include product data beyond the GTIN, such as the batch/lot number, serial number, best before date and expiration date. It also allows users, solution providers and GS1 Member Organisations to easily view, search and share details about individual Application Identifiers through web-browsers or on a mobile device. {br}{TOC}

Virtual printers are a useful developer and testing tool as they allow you to see the final output of your label without having to waste any label stock or ink ribbons. Virtual printers emulate the printing of any label type or size and the printing is done within seconds. {br}
==Installation== To begin, you will need to install a virtual printer emulator. The printer emulator you will install can be found on GitHub called [https://github.com/porrey/Virtual-ZPL-Printer|Virtual Zpl Printer]. To download, simply follow the hyperlink.
Once the application is downloaded, do the following: # Navigate to '''Windows Settings''' > '''Devices '''> '''Printers & Scanners''' and add a Printer using an IP address or hostname. # Select the '''TCP/IP device''' in Device Type. To find the Hostname, open the ''Virtual Zpl Printer'' emulator. Click on “Edit” in the top right corner, the IP Address is displayed in the IP Address section. The IP address you want to copy into the printer set up window will be the first option available when clicking on IP Address: 127.0.0.1 The port name will be the TCP Port found below the IP Address section. [image:b071ddb7-a41a-4386-b3a9-19de3a0d86e9|popup|center|Where to find the hostname and port number|300px] # Press '''next''', windows will be looking for your printer, however, you should be prompted to provide additional port information. # In Device Type, select '''Custom''' > '''Settings'''. # Make sure the '''IP Address''' (Hostname) and the '''Port Number''' correspond to the ones in your ''Virtual Zpl Printer'' settings, and the '''RAW''' protocol must be selected. # Click '''OK''', then '''Next'''. # When prompted to install printer drivers, select '''Generic''' > '''Generic/Text Only''' driver. If you already have printer driver downloaded, given they are for your physical Zebra compatible printers, these drivers will work fine as well. [image:47aec51b-1968-4d9a-8dec-1c4a251544d1|popup|center|Driver|350px] # Click '''Next '''> keep the recommended option > Click '''Next'''. # Name your printer > Click '''Next'''. #Regarding printer sharing, that will depend on your preference. # Click '''Finish'''.
You've completed the set up of the virtual printer. All that is left is connecting the printer to your DeviceHub. For more information on how to set up the connection with DeviceHub, follow the [236e58a0-0f90-429b-9a30-ad09bfcb5f93|Integration Guide]. The Asgard Labels functionality in Acumatica ERP provides a way to print labels from anywhere in Acumatica. Through Asgard Labels, you can also create your own label models with varying complexities and with different sets of rules to assist you in the printing process. {br} This guide will introduce you to the many screens that will help you create and render your desired labels and provide details on the proper configuration steps to associate users to labels they can print. Asgard Labels is a solution made with the idea that it will fulfill almost all labeling use cases. Being directly integrated within Acumatica, this solution has access to all Acumatica screens and data found within your Acumatica system. You can populate your label with any data found in your database, including User Defined fields and System Attributes. This is done by simply mapping variables found on your label to specifics fields from a screen. {br}
==Label Models==
A label model is a configuration associated with printing labels from an Acumatica screen. Label models is the form where all the parameter associated to the label creation process are set.
There are 3 types of label models: *Single label: A typical label associated with a screen where the label content can be configured and associated to screen expressions and users. *Group label: A list of screen related labels that can be all printed with a single click. *Snippets: A piece of label content that is used by an iterator to print multiple rows associated with a record (i.e. box items).
Label models can use any printing language and uses a fast, powerful, safe and lightweight scripting (templating) language with hundreds of functions and operators, called Scriban. In other words, label templates can be written with any printing language or you can use scriban functions. Both methods will provide you with your custom label that is ready to use from any screen you desire. Every model is mapped to a screen and from that screen, it must be linked to a view, which the label model will be able to pull data from. Label models follow a specific format, which you can create according to your specification, and can be given a margin and layout.
((({S:Warn}Only ZPL II, the Zebra Programming Language can be rendered at this time.)))

You use this form to view, configure, and create label dimensions and orientation. A label format describes the physical characteristics of a physical label and the printer configuration expected to print this label. Labels have different widths and heights and may be printed on printers having different printing densities (dots per inches or mm), qualities and orientations. For example, a classic example would be a 4 x 6 inches label with a density of 8 dots per mm (203 dots per in). In order to simplify those combinations, you can create as many formats as needed and re-use them across multiple label models. When the formats are created, the corresponding label format will be visible on the Format ID selector found in Label Models (~/?ScreenId=AL201000 AL201000) summary area.

The rendered barcode is displays the value inputted in the Sample Value text box. |- | '''Change ID''' | Gives you the ability to change the ID of the currently selected Barcode. |- | '''Load Default Barcodes''' | Loads all the barcodes found in the ZPL II programming guide at their default setting. Element !width="80%" ! Description |- | '''Barcode ID''' | The unique identifier of the barcode. If barcodes are loaded from the toolbar button ''Load Default Barcodes'', then the unique identifier are generated automatically by the system by taking the second character of the barcode command given from the ZPL II language command. |- | '''Description''' | A brief description of the type of barcode and its specific options (if applicable) for differentiation. |- | '''Barcode Type''' | The different types of barcodes featured in the ZPL II programming guide. There are a total of 31 barcode types available for processing by Zebra printers. |- | '''Sample Value''' | The value used in the rendering process of the barcode. Sample values are independent of the values used for printing. |- | '''Render Message''' | The messages or warnings displayed in case of a rendering issue. |- | '''Active'' | A check box that indicates (if selected) that the barcode is active in the system |- | '''Export'' | A check box that includes (if selected) the barcode to the export all file. |- | '''Language''' | The printer control language of the defined barcode. |- | '''Dimension''' | The dimension that the barcode can take. The following options are available: *''1D'': One-Dimensional Barcodes are linear codes that contain alphanumeric data. Varying in width lines and spaces, the information is encoded horizontally from left to right. 1D barcodes are dependent on connectivity to a database for the information to be meaningful. *''2D'': Two-Dimensional Barcodes uses patterns, shapes, and dots to encrypt information both horizontally and vertically. Due to their structure, 2D barcodes can hold more data than 1D barcodes, and are independent of a database connection to display the information. *''Postal'': Postal Barcodes are a series of long and short vertical bars, encoded horizontally. They are typically used by postal services and represent ZIP Codes, ZIP+4 codes and delivery addresses. *''Composite'': Composite Barcodes are GS1 barcodes that consists of a composite of barcode dimensions. ==Virtual Printers== When it comes to testing the printing of your labels, virtual printers are a useful developer and testing tool as they allow you to see the final output of your label without having to waste any label stock or ink ribbons. Virtual printers emulate the printing of any label type or size and the printing is done within seconds. This can be useful when testing the expressions assigned to the variables you set in your label model. By having a virtual printer, you can print the output of your label without having to print on physical label stock. For additional information on virtual printers and how to install them, you can view the following article: [96f8f2d3-bb09-461f-851b-ef259485cb1b|How to Install a Virtual Printer].

Form ID: (~/?ScreenId=AL201000 AL201000)
On this form, you can create, view, and edit label models. Label models are the labels that you will be printing and using to stick on whichever product, container, or box. You can render labels with the Render button and view the label that was defined in the Template tab. The rendering depends on certain settings on the Labels Preferences (~/?ScreenId=AL101000 AL101000) form. By default, the Labelary API is used and the programming language for the label template is Zebra.
Form Toolbar
The form toolbar includes standard and form-specific buttons and commands. For the list of standard buttons, see Form Toolbar. The form-specific commands (which can be shown as buttons on the form toolbar, as commands on the More menu, or in both places) are listed in the following table in alphabetical order.
Summary Area The summary tab is split into two sections. In the Summary area, you can select an existing label model by its model ID or specify summary information about a new label model. The right side displays the rendered label as an image, with the sample values entered in the Expression Tab. You can click on the rendered image to enlarge the label as a popup on your screen.
Template Tab This tab displays the label template, in a text edit. Templates can be written in a mixture of programming languages (ZPL, EPL, IPL, etc.) and the scripting language scriban; however, the template can also be written with strictly scriban functions and expressions. This is achieved by writing variables that are placed between brackets and the data contained within the variable can be configured in the expression tab.
Expression Tab The Expression tab contains the list of variables found from the label template through the scriban brace expressions. Given that the label is mapped to a screen, variables pulled from the views of said screen may be used as assignable values for printing. In this version, all the data configuration and variable mapping is done in this tab.
Table Toolbar
The table toolbar includes standard buttons and buttons that are specific to this table. For the list of standard buttons, see Table Toolbar. The table-specific buttons are listed below.
Table Columns

Table Columns Rendered Tab The Rendered tab allows you to see the ZPL output of your label model. On top of seeing the ZPL code of your model, you can also see the Label Name, the GUID of the user who created the model, and the current graph.
Setup Tab The Setup tab allows you to setup different filters and descriptors for your model.

On this form, you can create, view, and edit colors that you want to place on labels. Colors can be used on Label Models (~/?ScreenId=AL201000 AL201000) to allow your label to enhance communication and differentiate. In other words, you can use colors to your labels to convey a particular meaning to warehouse workers or distributors. For instance, red could signify warning or hazardous products, green could be eco-friendly, etc. Colors can also allow your labels to stand out from the standard black and white label.
